question: Which song by The Beatles starts with a chord jump from the tonic to the minor fitfh chord?

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The jump that is normally cited in the Beatles literature is the opening of A Hard Day’s Night.

In the recorded version the song is in G major and the first struck harmony is the G-major tonic, the famous ‘A Hard Day’s Night’ guitar chord. The music immediately moves on to the harmony that sits on the fifth degree of the scale, G – D, and in this case it is heard as the minor-mode v, D minor / E minor in the common transcriptions of the riff, i.e. a tonic → v move. In the more usual theoretical description of the Beatles’ own I–v opening the clearest textbook example is the E-major opening of Happiness Is a Warm Gun, E major tonic to B minor v, the I–v tonic-to-minor-fifth opening that is often quoted for the I–v type jump. That is the I–v tonic–minor-fifth opening most writers refer to for the group.

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The opening that is most often cited for the I → v jump is the
E-major opening of Helter Skelter / Can't Buy Me Love / the A-major family of
early Beatles numbers.

In the key that the song is normally quoted in the first two sounding
harmonies are the tonic and its diatonic fifth, the fifth degree being
minor in a major key.  In E that is

   E major  –  B minor

E = I in E major and Bm = v in E major, i.e. the root moves a perfect fifth
up, I → v, the characteristic tonic-to-minor-fifth jump that opens the
record.  The same root motion is heard in the A-major idiom that the group
uses for the early A-major numbers, e.g. Can't Buy Me Love / A Hard Day's
Night / I Should Have Known Better, A major → E minor I → v, the textbook
Beatles I-to-minor-v opening. That is the I→v tonic-to-minor-fifth jump that
is normally quoted for the band.

8.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: In the Beatles canon the clearest textbook i–v opening is the
string-quartet intro to Eleanor Rigby.

The piece is in E natural minor. The opening two string chords are

* E minor = i, the tonic
* B minor = v, the minor triad built on the 5th degree of E natural minor

So the music opens with a perfect-fifth root movement i → v, the tonic
jumping up a fifth to the diatonic minor fifth chord.  It is the
i–v motion that gives the piece its stark, open string-quartet sound
Em – Bm – C – ... before the vocal enters.

*Remark on the tritone reading.* If you mean the literal interval a
minor fifth / tritone up from the tonic, the Beatles’ textbook tritone
I – ♭V / #ii opening is Come Together, famously C – F♯/G♭ minor in the
intro riff “Here come old flat-top…”, i.e. the tonic C jumping a
diminished 5th/minor 6th to the chord a tritone away.

6.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The opening you are thinking of is the tritone / I – ♭V leap that the band use to open Come Together, and it is the same sort of device that is most often quoted for the piano intro of A Day in the Life.

In the normal concert-pitch rendering the tune is treated as being centred on E. The first sound the listener actually hears is the tonic E – in the record essentially an E minor colour held by the bass – and the riff then moves immediately to the note/chord a tritone/minor fifth away, G♭, i.e. the ♭V/ the “minor-fifth” chord of the tonic. That E → G♭/E → ♭V jump, a tonic-to-tritone leap, is the shock opening of the Come Together riff and is the classic Beatles illustration of a tonic-to-minor-fifth tritone jump. The same I → ♭V tritone idea is the one most often quoted for the E-major piano opening of A Day in the Life, the famous E-major–based opening that falls to the tritone region on the first lyric.

2.text:
The most often quoted Beatles opening of the sort is the opening of
A Hard Day’s Night.

In G major the piece is set up on the G tonic and the first real
harmonic move of the verse / intro is a big leap down a fifth to the
v chord of the key. In the recording the G-major tonic is stated and
is immediately answered by the E-minor / D-minor area that is heard
as the v – the minor fifth degree – of the G major / E minor
central tonality.  It is that I → v, tonic-to-the-minor-fifth, leap,
a fifth down from G to the minor fifth degree of the key, that gives
the song its famously abrupt “jump” opening.

The same I→v opening is the one that is usually cited for the
‘Strawberry Fields Forever’ / A Hard Day’s Night family of openings,
e.g. the A-major → E-minor I→v leap with which Strawberry Fields
Forever is normally analysed, A major tonic to the v chord E minor a
perfect fifth below. That is the Beatles I–v tonic-to-minor-fifth
jump that is quoted in the theory literature.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The move you are describing is the I → v  modal-interchange
move that the group uses over and over on the White Album.

The textbook example is the White Album opening of *Dear Prudence*.
The piece is in E major and the finger-picked intro is

E – Bm – E – Bm – …

i.e. tonic E major jumping a perfect fifth up to B minor, the minor
v-degree of the key. The same I → v tonic-to-minor-fifth-degree jump is
the one that is normally quoted for the A-major opening of
*Strawberry Fields Forever*, A major → E minor I → v, and it is the
same move that opens *Dear Prudence* in E major, E major → B minor I → v.

3.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The trick that is normally pointed out in this connection is the opening of
Come Together.

The tune is normally heard in D / D minor and the famous riff is
presented as a tonic – ♭V / “minor-fifth’’  jump.  In the recorded
version the guitar / bass statement opens on the tonic D and is
immediately answered a tritone away on A♭, the flattened fifth/
diminished/minor-fifth of D, D → A♭.  It is that D → A♭/G♯m
I – ♭V/ v  gesture – the tonic leaping a tritone/minor-fifth to the
chord a tritone away – that gives the song its characteristic
unsettled, bluesy opening and is the Beatles’ textbook example of a
tonic-to-minor-fifth/♭V opening jump. The same I–v flavour is the
one that is popularly quoted for the A-hard-Day’s-Night-type openings
in the literature, e.g. G – Eｍ I –v in G, the tonic leaping to its
minor fifth.

6.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The question is ambiguous between “tonic → the diatonic v chord, i.e. the fifth degree which is minor in a major key” and “tonic → a chord a minor-fifth / tritone away, i.e. I → ♭V”. The round-0 discussion is split on that distinction.

I-v / tonic-to-minor-fifth-degree claims:
* A Hard Day’s Night is repeatedly cited as the textbook I → v opening. Colleague 2/4 describe it in G major as G tonic jumping to the minor fifth-degree area E minor/D minor, described as the famous abrupt jump. Colleague 1 places the same root motion in the A-major family: A major → E minor I → v for A Hard Day’s Night / Can’t Buy Me Love / I Should Have Known Better, and E major → B minor I → v for Helter Skelter / Can’t Buy Me Love-type numbers.
* Strawberry Fields Forever is linked to the same A major → E minor I → v leap by Colleagues 2 and 7.
* Dear Prudence is given as a clear White Album example E major → B minor I → v, tonic a perfect fifth up to the minor v-degree, Colleague 7.
* Happiness Is a Warm Gun is also offered as E major tonic to B minor v by Colleague 4.
* Eleanor Rigby is offered as i → v in E natural minor: Em = i, Bm = v, a perfect-fifth root movement up, Colleague 8.

Tritone / I → ♭V / tonic-to-minor-fifth-interval claims:
* Come Together is the most repeated tritone candidate. Colleague 3: D tonic → A♭/G♯m, D → A♭ tritone/minor-fifth I – ♭V. Colleague 6: centred on E, E → G♭/♭V tritone jump, and notes the same I→♭V idea is quoted for A Day in the Life’s E-major opening. Colleague 8’s remark on the tritone reading gives Come Together as C → F♯/G♭ minor, tonic jumping a diminished 5th/minor 6th to the chord a tritone away.
* Colleague 6 also links A Day in the Life piano intro to the E → G♭ ♭V tritone idea.

Disagreements / problems noticed:
* G → E minor is not the diatonic v of G major; v in G is D minor. E minor is vi. Several colleagues treat E minor as “the minor fifth” in a modal/mix context, suggesting confusion between v and vi/relative minor.
* Come Together transposition is inconsistent across colleagues: D → A♭ vs E → G♭ vs C → F♯/G♭. The tritone relationship holds but the nominal tonic key is disputed.
* Colleague 1 conflates several early E/A-major numbers; Helter Skelter’s opening is not a clean I→v chord jump in the same way as Dear Prudence.

Current belief state: The I → v perfect-fifth tonic-to-minor-fifth-degree opening is a real Beatles trope and the most cited textbook instances are A Hard Day’s Night / Strawberry Fields Forever / Dear Prudence with A → E minor and E → B minor. The tritone I → ♭V “minor-fifth interval” reading points most strongly to Come Together. Unresolved is which reading the question intends: diatonic v vs intervallic minor fifth/tritone. Need clarification on “minor fitfh chord” meaning minor-fifth degree vs minor-fifth interval, before committing to a single song.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The discussion is split between two different readings of “tonic to the minor fifth chord” and between several candidate songs.

* I → v perfect-fifth root motion to the diatonic minor fifth degree
  * Colleague 1,4,7 cite the E-major → B-minor family: Helter Skelter / Happiness Is a Warm Gun / Dear Prudence E – Bm – E – Bm…; also A-major → E-minor family: Can’t Buy Me Love / A Hard Day’s Night / I Should Have Known Better / Strawberry Fields Forever A – Em.
  * Colleague 2,4 cite A Hard Day’s Night as the archetypal I → v opening in G major, described as G tonic followed by the minor fifth-degree harmony, with an allied Strawberry Fields Forever A → Em analysis.
  * Colleague 7 singles out White Album Dear Prudence in E major, E major jumping a perfect fifth up to B minor, the v degree, as the textbook White-Album example, and notes the same motion for Strawberry Fields Forever.
  * Colleague 8 notes Eleanor Rigby’s string-quartet intro in E natural minor, i → v : E minor = i, B minor = v, a perfect-fifth root movement Em – Bm – C…
  * Colleague 4 also mentions Happiness Is a Warm Gun E major → B minor v as a textbook I–v quote.

* Tritone / ♭V “minor-fifth interval” reading
  * Colleague 3,6 argue for Come Together as the classic tonic-to-minor-fifth / tritone jump. Colleague 3 describes D → A♭ / G♯m I – ♭V/v; Colleague 6 describes the riff centred on E as E → G♭/♭V, and links the same I → ♭V idea to A Day in the Life’s E-major piano opening.
  * Colleague 8 adds a remark: if the literal minor-fifth/tritone interval is intended, the textbook Beatles tritone I – ♭V/#ii is Come Together, famously C → F♯/G♭ minor.

Disagreements and points needing check:
* The exact harmony of A Hard Day’s Night is contested in the thread: G → Em/Dm is described as v, but v of G major is D minor, Em is vi. Colleague 2’s G → Em/Dm area is inconsistent.
* Transposition confusion for Come Together: D → A♭ vs E → G♭ vs C → F♯. The tritone reading is agreed as Come Together, but the key naming varies.
* Multiple songs fit the I → v perfect-fifth description: Dear Prudence E→Bm, Happiness Is a Warm Gun E→Bm, A Hard Day’s Night / Can’t Buy Me Love A→Em, Eleanor Rigby Em→Bm. No consensus on which is the intended unique example.
* Colleague 5 gave no response.

Unresolved: whether the question means v = diatonic minor fifth degree reached by a perfect fifth root motion, or ♭V reached by a minor-fifth/tritone interval. The public pool contains strong support for both A Hard Day’s Night/Dear Prudence I→v and Come Together I→♭V tritone. I need to keep both families in mind and clarify the interval vs scale-degree interpretation before committing.

* Colleague 4 adds Happiness Is a Warm Gun E-major → B-minor as a clear textbook I→v example.
* Colleague 7 points to Dear Prudence, White Album, E-major arpeggiated E – Bm – E – Bm as I→v, and equates it with the A-major → E-minor opening of Strawberry Fields Forever.
* Colleague 8 notes Eleanor Rigby string-quartet intro in E natural minor i → v: E-minor = i, B-minor = v, a perfect-fifth root move, and distinguishes it from the tritone reading.

I → ♭V / tonic-to-tritone “minor-fifth interval” camp:
* Colleague 3 and 6 identify Come Together as the tonic-to-minor-fifth/tritone jump. Colleague 3 describes D → A♭/G♯m I – ♭V/ v, Colleague 6 describes E → G♭ ♭V tritone and links the same idea to A Day in the Life’s piano intro.
* Colleague 8 remarks that if the literal interval a minor fifth/tritone up from the tonic is intended, the Beatles textbook tritone I – ♭V/#ii opening is Come Together, famously circa C – F♯/G♭.

Conflicts / errors to track:
* A Hard Day’s Night chord identity is inconsistently described as G → E-minor vs G → D-minor; the exact verse harmony needs verification.
* Some colleagues conflate I→v perfect-fifth move with the tritone I→♭V move, using “minor fifth” for both.

A major → E minor I → v : Strawberry Fields Forever, Can’t Buy Me Love / I Should Have Known Better

The deliberation remains locked on the lexical fork of “minor fifth chord” and round 4 shows no convergence, only explicit dual maintenance of both readings.

Reading A – conventional Beatles theory shorthand
* minor fifth chord = the diatonic fifth degree which is minor in a major key, i.e. v, reached by a perfect-fifth root motion I → v, not a tritone motion.
* Family is ubiquitous and repeatedly cited:
  E major → B minor I → v: Dear Prudence White Album E – Bm – E – Bm …, Happiness Is a Warm Gun, Helter Skelter;
  A major → E minor I → v: Strawberry Fields Forever, Can’t Buy Me Love / I Should Have Known Better;
  G major → v family: A Hard Day’s Night, transcription unstable in thread G → E minor / D minor;
  natural-minor parallel i → v: Eleanor Rigby Em → Bm.
* Dear Prudence E → Bm is the chord-by-chord verifiable, transcriptionally unambiguous major-mode realisation of the move. A Hard Day’s Night / Strawberry Fields Forever is the culturally iconic name most often repeated for the whole I → v trope. Colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,7,8 keep this as the intended sense and note the wording “to the minor fifth chord” rather than “a chord a minor fifth away” is the normal theory shorthand.

Reading B – literal interval reading
* a chord whose root is a minor fifth / tritone away from the tonic = I → ♭V / #ii, a tritone root motion.
* Canonical unanimous Beatles example in the thread: Come Together, D-centred D → A♭/G♯m, concert-pitch E → G♭ ♭V, the classic tonic-to-tritone shock. Same I–♭V device is linked to the E-major piano intro of A Day in the Life and the “Here come old flat-top…” riff.
* Colleagues 2,5,6 explicitly argue the natural-language phrasing points to the tritone interval. Colleague 6 in round 4 states the wording “a chord jump … to the minor fifth chord” is most naturally read in ordinary language as an intervallic minor-fifth/tritone jump, i.e. I → ♭V.

Disagreements / ambiguities persisting
* Whether setter means diatonic v-degree minor quality reached by perfect-fifth root motion, or a chord a minor-fifth/tritone interval away from tonic.
* Within I → v camp no single song agreed as sole answer: A Hard Day’s Night is most repeated name, Dear Prudence is analytically cleanest E–Bm instantiation, Strawberry Fields Forever / Can’t Buy Me Love are A–E minor representatives. Transcription instability noted for A Hard Day’s Night.

Current belief
The question is ambiguous and the group is stable on the bifurcation. If taken in conventional Beatles theory shorthand as diatonic fifth degree which is minor in a major, the most frequently cited exemplars are the A Hard Day’s Night / Dear Prudence / Strawberry Fields Forever I → v family, with Dear Prudence E–Bm as the most analytically clean realisation and A Hard Day’s Night as the most often named single song. If taken literally as a minor-fifth/tritone interval away from tonic, the canonical example is Come Together D → A♭ / E → G♭ I → ♭V. Both readings remain defensible with strong colleague support and unresolved which interpretation the setter intends; the literal-interval reading is explicitly argued as linguistically faithful to the phrasing in round 4, while a majority of colleagues continue to maintain the conventional diatonic v reading as the intended sense.
